linkages: An encrypted ID for fathers and mothers allows for matching a child's DNT test score to the Danish registers that reflect the police and criminal records of their parents (p. 5).
Encrypted IDs also allow for linking to other administrative registers that include information on the child's background characteristics and the parents' socioeconomic status (p. 5).

sample.universe: Children of compulsory school age (up to about 15) taking the Danish National Test in 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th and/or 8th grade from 2010 to 2014; the DNT covers about 95% of this full population (N = 603,380 children), linked to full-population Danish register data.
sample.unit_of_observation: child (one DNT test observation per child)
selection_rules: Children who experienced parental incarceration for the first time between age 0 and 9th grade (about age 15): N = 17,401 children.
Children who experience PI up to one year before the test date or up to one year after the test date: remaining N = 2,099 children.
Paternal incarceration only (maternal incarcerations excluded): remaining N = 1,891 children.
Analysis samples: 1,718 children with a reading test score (940 PI pre, 778 PI post) and 909 children with a math test score (505 PI pre, 404 PI post).
School absence analysis: children in public schools with absence information for the 10 months before and after PI, N = 612.
Table 3 samples are defined analogously for each form of paternal justice involvement (N between 620 and 5,960).
sample.n_observations: 1,718 children (reading test score); 909 children (math test score)
sample.n_individuals: 1,891 children after the three sample restrictions

construction_notes: All test scores are z-standardized by sex, grade and cohort; raw DNT scores range from 1 to 100 (p. 6).
Reading test outcomes pool 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th grade; math test outcomes pool 3rd and 6th grade (p. 6).
The treatment is a dummy: 1 = PI within 1 year before the test, 0 = PI within 1 year after the test (p. 6).
If the father is in pretrial incarceration before his sentenced incarceration starts, the start date of the incarceration is the first date of the pretrial incarceration (p. 6).
Jail stays of less than 24 h are not included in the main analyses (footnote 1, p. 4).
Covariates for parents' characteristics are measured when the child is age 6, to ensure they are measured before the parent is incarcerated (p. 6).
The models control for the time between test and PI, measured in days (p. 6).

High school absence is defined as more than 10% school absence within a month; results are given for unexcused absence and for all types of absence; July is missing from the absence data because of summer holidays (p. 7 and footnote 4).
In the additional analysis for pretrial incarcerations, only pretrial incarcerations that did not lead to a prison sentence are included (p. 7).
For the 'criminal act' analysis, only criminal acts that led to a criminal charge are included (footnote 5, p. 7).
For the distributional analysis, DNT test scores are divided into 20 quantiles (5% each) and a linear probability model is run for each quantile (p. 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimate is interpreted as the joint impact of incarceration (physical separation from the child) and its subsequent consequences, relative to children who have 'only' experienced the disadvantages leading up to incarceration; the authors do not claim causal evidence.

threats_discussed: Selection bias: both the causes and the consequences of parental incarceration likely produce educational problems, so instability preceding PI may drive any association (Section 2.1, p. 3).
Anticipation: children in the control group may already know their father is at risk of a prison sentence, which may itself be a stressor during the test (p. 6).
Classification error: the comparison group may contain children whose parent was incarcerated before they were born (p. 6).
Treatment heterogeneity: PI incorporates a heterogeneous set of experiences; 74% of fathers of treated children were already released at the test date (p. 6).

Imbalance: the father has been charged with a domestic offence for 14% of treated vs 11% of control children in the reading sample (p < .05), and domestic violence is correlated with poor educational outcomes (p. 8).
The authors acknowledge that test score declines appear to begin prior to PI (p. 11).
robustness_checks: Propensity score matching with a nearest neighbour approach (Table B1): results similar to Table 2, but the standard error increases and the reading estimate becomes insignificant (p. 9).
Only prison sentences, excluding pretrial incarceration (Table B2): same conclusion; the reading estimates even increase slightly (p. 9).
Younger (2nd and 4th grade) vs older (6th and 8th grade) cohorts separately (Table B3): -0.130 vs -0.069, not significantly different (p = .367) (p. 9).
Parental incarceration including maternal incarceration (Table B4): reading estimates slightly smaller and insignificant (footnote 6, p. 9).
Test scores not standardized by sex (Table B5): results similar (footnote 6, p. 9).
Models with and without covariates reported side by side in Table 2; estimates and standard errors are rather similar across them (p. 8).
Regression models with covariates for school absence (Fig. B2): no peak in school absence the exact month the father starts his incarceration (p. 9).
unresolved_confounders: The authors cannot completely reject that the measured differences in reading test scores are also driven by factors other than PI (p. 10).
Control-group children may already suspect a looming incarceration, so part of the response to PI may already be present in the comparison group (p. 6).
Danish registry data do not include a rich set of measures of family life that might predict parental incarceration (p. 2).

Regression models with covariates for school absence (Fig. B2): no peak in school absence the exact month the father starts his incarceration (p. 9).
unresolved_confounders: The authors cannot completely reject that the measured differences in reading test scores are also driven by factors other than PI (p. 10).
Control-group children may already suspect a looming incarceration, so part of the response to PI may already be present in the comparison group (p. 6).
Danish registry data do not include a rich set of measures of family life that might predict parental incarceration (p. 2).
